heading: 25 October 2026 — shared-power restriction and conventional routing closeout
body:
25 October 2026 — shared-power restriction and conventional routing closeout
The frozen one-axis experiment is complete. Four exposed FIT groups were evaluated with grid power 90 versus 45 kW, holding all other physical parameters and each group's original source0 fleet quantity fixed. Eight fresh fixed-reference feasibility acquisitions were attempted; five yielded timely independently replayed priors. Three 45 kW fixed-reference numerical models returned INFEASIBLE. Their six assigned fixed QP decisions remained missing, while all adaptive arms remained eligible cold. Of 32 planned active decisions, 26 were attempted, 22 admitted qualified physical QP endpoints, and 21 met the declared full-method-success flag. Administrative campaign closure does not mean complete methodological success.
The useful feasibility witness is group10006: conventional full-graph routing produced replay-valid five-bus alternatives under 45 kW at both tariffs, while its fixed reference topology returned native INFEASIBLE. These alternatives used about570.9889 kWh versus the reference topology's ideal555.5222 kWh. More energy accompanied feasible access to charging opportunities. This establishes those new witnesses, not a global infeasibility certificate or proof that rerouting was necessary. At45 kW, the two other cold adaptive groups (10009 and10005) returned INF_OR_UNBD with no incumbent or QP; they remain unresolved rather than being labeled physically infeasible. No retry, cap retuning or outcome replacement occurred.
The intended aggregate cost interaction is unavailable: only10 of16 resource-by-tariff blocks and2 of8 paired interactions are defined, so the frozen complete-cohort mean is null. Only10001 is complete at both resources. Under flat source0 prices its fixed-minus-adaptive point gains were0.195301 cost units at90 kW and0.163498 at45 kW, giving interaction -0.031803; source1 differences and interaction were around numerical roundoff. The restriction therefore did not increase the observed cost benefit in that one complete group. We do not substitute a survivor-only mean for the missing study-wide result.
A small load-spreading tradeoff is explicit in10001/source0. The adaptive route used505.7333 rather than500.3333 kWh, increasing linear electricity cost from100.0667 to101.1467, but reducing the quadratic supply component from11.5895 to10.3142 at90 kW. The reduction outweighed extra energy at unchanged fleet and zero deadhead cost. This is a returned conventional-policy mechanism, not a learned gain or exact ideal routing optimum. Other baseline contrasts, including a negative adaptive gain and a routing-no-incumbent fallback, remain preserved.
All four reference systems returned before terminal opening1080, but only10001 met the sufficient no-midday-SOC condition. The other three reference demands exceed the540 kWh terminal-only capacity at45 kW and require daytime opportunities; none of the four fits the cheap-only sufficient range. Window counts and failed sufficient conditions are not feasibility proofs. A separately frozen analytical necessary-capacity-cut diagnostic is the next justified direction before more solver or training work. Existing derived diagnostics may suffice without reopening TRAIN plans. No such calculation is launched by this closeout, and classical energy/window cuts are not claimed as new theorems.
The owner and one compact readout used150.97 displayed CPU seconds and157.62 elapsed-sum seconds, within the selected4500 CPU/7200 wall package. Exact costs, physical components, failures, native scopes, all planned denominators and historical unknown charges are preserved. Ideal route ordering and the unresolved cold cases are not promoted to full-space certificates. The earlier failed practical learning increment for both families remains unchanged; no automatic refit or manuscript-readiness claim follows.
